subject: Historia
title: Industrialisation in Sweden
sourceSummary: How Sweden, during the second half of the 1800s, moved from an agricultural society to an industrial society: railways, inventions and factories, the move into the cities, new working conditions, and the popular movements that ordinary people built up.
topics: from agricultural society to industrial society

questions.topic: from agricultural society to industrial society
questions.prompt: Which goods were most important to the breakthrough of Swedish industry during the second half of the 1800s?
questions.opener: Think about which raw materials Sweden had plenty of in its forests and mountains.
choices: Cotton and silk
Cars and aeroplanes
Timber, iron and later wood pulp
Coffee, sugar and spices
questions.explanation: Sweden's industrialisation was built on the country's own raw materials: sawn timber for Europe's cities, iron from Bergslagen and, from the 1870s, wood pulp. Cotton and silk were British and Asian goods, while cars and aeroplanes belonged to the 1900s.

questions.prompt: What did the expansion of the railway from the 1850s onwards mean most for Sweden?
questions.opener: Compare it with how goods were transported before: on poor roads or on water that froze in winter.
choices: Goods and people could be transported quickly and cheaply over long distances all year round
All Swedes could start travelling abroad on holiday
Farming could be abandoned entirely
The cities stopped growing because people could stay in the countryside
questions.explanation: The railway linked forests, mines and ironworks with ports and cities, and it kept running through winter even when lakes and canals were frozen over – this lowered transport costs and tied the market together. Cities, on the contrary, grew faster, and farming remained the largest industry well into the 1900s.

questions.prompt: Which Swedish inventor became world-famous for dynamite and then founded the Nobel Prizes?
questions.opener: This surname is announced every year on 10 December.
choices: Gustaf de Laval
Lars Magnus Ericsson
Jonas Wenström
Alfred Nobel
questions.explanation: Alfred Nobel patented dynamite in 1867 and left his fortune to the prizes that bear his name. De Laval developed the milk separator, Ericsson built telephones, and Wenström worked on generators – important inventors, but not of dynamite.

questions.opener: The word comes from "stat" – the payment received in goods instead of money.
choices: Farmers who owned their own farm
Farm labourers who were employed with their whole family for one year at a time and paid mostly in kind, for example milk and housing
Government officials in the countryside
Soldiers who were given a cottage by the state
questions.explanation: "Statare" were farm labourers hired by the family on one-year contracts and paid mostly in kind – milk, grain and housing in a "statare" cottage row. Farmers who owned their land had their own house and fields, and soldiers' cottages belonged to the older military allotment system.

questions.prompt: What was the temperance movement's main goal?
questions.opener: The movement's name refers to a drink that caused big problems in many homes.
choices: To build more factories in the countryside
To make sure all children could go to school
To reduce the harm caused by alcohol in society
To get women the right to vote
questions.explanation: The temperance movement, with organisations such as IOGT and the Blue Ribbon movement, wanted to reduce drinking and the social problems – poverty, illness and insecurity in families – that alcohol brought with it. The question of suffrage was driven above all by the suffrage movement and the labour movement, even though many members were involved in several movements.

questions.prompt: Why are the labour movement, the temperance movement and the free-church movement called "popular movements" (folkrörelser)?
questions.opener: Think about who started them – did the initiative come from above or from below?
choices: They were built up by ordinary people who organised themselves in associations across the whole country
They were founded by the king and parliament
They were run by the Church of Sweden
They consisted only of members from the cities' bourgeoisie
questions.explanation: Popular movements are characterised by ordinary people joining together voluntarily in local associations, choosing their own leaders, holding meetings and learning to speak, write and organise – a school in democracy. The free churches, by contrast, grew up in opposition to the state church, and the movements were based among workers and smallholders rather than the bourgeoisie.

questions.prompt: Explain how life for an ordinary Swedish family changed between 1850 and 1900.
questions.opener: Follow the family from the farm to the city: work, housing, the children's days and the chance to have a say.
questions.answer: In 1850 most Swedes lived in the countryside and lived off farming, often as tenant farmers, "statare" or farm labourers, with tasks that followed the seasons and pay partly in kind. By 1900 the population had grown sharply, farming had become more efficient, and industry had created new jobs in cities and mill towns. Many families therefore moved into cities such as Stockholm, Gothenburg and Norrköping, where they took up wage work with fixed hours, long working days and overcrowding in tenement housing. At the same time, new opportunities grew: the elementary school gave children literacy, the railway and the postal service shortened distances, and in trade unions, temperance lodges and free churches ordinary people could organise and demand change.
steps: Starting point in 1850: an agricultural society, work following the seasons, pay partly in kind, high child mortality.
Population growth and more efficient farming meant there was not enough land for everyone – many became landless.
Industry and the railway created new jobs in cities and mill towns, which attracted people to move.
In the city, life became wage work by the clock with long days, overcrowding, and dependence on wages stretching to cover food and rent.
New institutions and movements – the elementary school, trade unions, the temperance movement and the free churches – gave knowledge, community and a chance to have a say.

questions.topic: from agricultural society to industrial society
questions.opener: Think timing, raw materials, inventions, cities, working conditions and popular movements.
questions.answer: Sweden industrialised later than Britain, above all from the 1850s onwards · the basis was its own raw materials: sawn timber, iron from Bergslagen and, from the 1870s, wood pulp · the railway was built out from 1856 and linked forests, mines, ironworks and ports all year round · Swedish inventors and companies: Alfred Nobel (dynamite), Gustaf de Laval (the separator), Lars Magnus Ericsson (telephones), later ASEA and SKF · urbanisation: people moved from the countryside to cities and mill towns, Stockholm and Gothenburg grew fast · working conditions: long working days, low wages, risk of accidents, child labour and overcrowding in tenement housing · in the countryside there were tenant farmers and "statare", who were paid in kind · class divisions were large between workers and factory owners · popular movements grew up from below: the labour movement with trade unions and social democracy, the temperance movement against the harms of alcohol, and the free churches outside the state church · the popular movements became a school in democracy and drove demands for the right to vote, better working conditions and social reforms.

questions.prompt: What was common regarding child labour in early Swedish factories?
questions.opener: Child labour legislation came in stages and offered children little protection at first.
choices: Child labour was completely banned as early as 1850
Only boys over 18 were allowed to work in factories
Children never worked in factories, only on farms
Children could work long days for low pay, especially in the textile industry
questions.explanation: In the early factories, not least in the textile industry, children did work long days for very low pay, before laws gradually began to restrict and later ban child labour. It was therefore neither completely banned as early as 1850 nor limited to adult boys or to farming alone.

questions.prompt: Which movement worked especially for better wages and working conditions for industrial workers through trade unions?
questions.opener: This movement later gave rise to its own political party.
choices: The temperance movement
The free-church movement
The suffrage movement for women only
The labour movement
questions.explanation: The labour movement organised industrial workers in trade unions to negotiate over wages and working conditions, and it later gained a political branch in the Social Democrats. The temperance movement and the free churches had other main concerns, and the women's suffrage movement was a separate, partly overlapping movement.

questions.topic: from agricultural society to industrial society
questions.prompt: What did the land reforms, such as "laga skifte", mean for Swedish farming during the 1800s?
questions.opener: Previously, a farm's land was often scattered in many narrow strips around the village.
choices: All land became state property
Farmers lost the right to own land
Farming was banned in favour of industry
Farmland was consolidated into fewer and larger connected plots instead of many small strips
questions.explanation: The land reforms merged a farm's previously scattered small strips into fewer and larger connected plots of land, making it easier to farm more efficiently. The reforms were thus about how the land was divided up, not about the state taking over ownership or farming being banned.

questions.prompt: Which company was founded by Lars Magnus Ericsson and later became a major international telecom company?
questions.opener: The company still carries its founder's surname.
choices: ASEA
SKF
Volvo
Ericsson
questions.explanation: Lars Magnus Ericsson founded the company that is today called Ericsson, which became one of the world's major telecom companies. ASEA (today part of ABB), SKF and Volvo were other important Swedish industrial companies but were founded by other people in other sectors.

questions.prompt: What was a common type of housing for factory workers in growing cities during industrialisation?
questions.opener: Many families had to make do with very little space.
choices: Large manor houses
Free villas from the state
Castles
Overcrowded tenement buildings
questions.explanation: Factory workers in growing cities often lived in overcrowded tenement buildings, sometimes with entire families in a single room. Manor houses and castles belonged to a completely different social class, and the state did not build free villas for working-class families during this period.

questions.prompt: Roughly how long could working days be for factory workers during early industrialisation?
questions.opener: Compare it with today's legally mandated eight-hour day.
choices: Never more than 6 hours
Exactly 8 hours by law
Only 4 hours a day
Often 10–12 hours or more
questions.explanation: Working days of 10–12 hours or more were common in early factories, long before laws on a standard working day were introduced. The eight-hour day did not become law in Sweden until 1919, after many years of demands from the labour movement.

questions.prompt: What did the suffrage movement fight for during the age of industrialisation?
questions.opener: The right to vote was long tied to gender, income and wealth.
choices: That only the nobility should be allowed to vote
To abolish all elections entirely
That only big cities should be allowed to vote
That more people, for example workers and women, should get the right to vote
questions.explanation: The suffrage movement demanded that the right to vote be extended to more groups who had previously been excluded, including propertyless workers and women, instead of only applying to men with sufficient income or wealth. So it wanted to broaden democracy, not restrict it to the nobility or to big cities.
